questions.q: What is the main advantage of structured (JSON) logging over plain-text log lines?
options: It uses less disk space
Every field becomes individually searchable and filterable instead of being buried in a sentence
It removes the need for timestamps
It makes logs unreadable to humans, which is more secure
questions.explain: Structured logs turn free-form text into named key-value fields, so a search tool can filter on level, service, or event directly instead of relying on fragile text matching.

questions.q: In a well-formed structured log line, what should the `level` field represent?
options: The server's CPU usage at the time of the log
A small, consistent severity label like debug, info, warn, error, or fatal
A random identifier for sorting
The number of microservices involved
questions.explain: A small fixed set of levels, used consistently, is what makes alerting on 'error rate' trustworthy — loose use of error leads to alert fatigue.

questions.q: What problem does a correlation ID solve?
options: It compresses log files automatically
It encrypts sensitive fields in logs
It ties together every log line written by every service that handled one specific request
It replaces the need for log levels
questions.explain: A correlation ID is generated once at the edge of the system and passed through every downstream service, so searching for it reconstructs the full story of one request across services.

questions.q: Why does newline-delimited JSON (one JSON object per line) matter for log files?
options: It's required by all programming languages
Log shippers and parsers read log files line by line, so one record per line keeps parsing reliable
It makes the file smaller than plain text
It's only a stylistic preference with no functional benefit
questions.explain: Log shipping and indexing tools expect one JSON object per line; pretty-printed JSON with embedded newlines breaks line-by-line parsing.

questions.q: At Northbridge Retail, a checkout request touches the checkout, inventory, payment, and notification services, each logging independently. What's the risk without a shared correlation ID?
options: The services would stop working entirely
Logs would be stored in the wrong timezone
Reconstructing what happened to that one request means guessing from timestamps across four separate, unlinked log streams
There is no risk — log levels solve this already
questions.explain: Without a correlation ID (or trace ID), there's no reliable field linking log lines across services, so engineers are left guessing based on approximate timing instead of following one request directly.
